title: Non-Stationarity in Financial Time Series: A Unifying Survey on Drift Detection, Adaptive Learning, and Evaluation
authors: Davi M. Cabral, Adriano M. A. Lima, Gustavo H. F. M. Oliveira, Adriano L. I. Oliveira
tldr: Surveys drift detection, adaptive learning, and evaluation for non-stationary financial time series, proposing a unified four-axis taxonomy and a five-pillar pipeline connecting representation, detection, adaptation, and evaluation.
problem_and_motivation: Financial time series are inherently non-stationary: distribution shifts, regime transitions, and structural breaks degrade model performance precisely when decisions matter most. The literature is fragmented across econometrics, statistical monitoring, and machine learning with divergent terminology and incompatible evaluation protocols, hindering cumulative evidence and practical adoption.
approach: Unified four-axis taxonomy of non-stationarity: temporal (how/when), statistical (what changes), spatial (where), and ontological (structure/state), with causal drivers as a foundational layer
Five-pillar pipeline: non-stationarity characterization, drift-aware representations (endogenous embeddings, exogenous context, multimodal), change detection, continuous adaptation, and evaluation
Layered representation approach spanning internal signals, exogenous context, latent regime structure, and downstream-task-oriented features
Review of change-detection methods: segmentation (PELT, Bai-Perron), sequential monitoring (CUSUM, EWMA, DDM), Bayesian (BOCPD, HMM), embedding-based OOD, and structural dependence methods
Adaptation strategies: parametric (TVP/Kalman, TAR/STAR, HMM), dynamic ensembles (gating, adaptive weighting, expert retirement), and hybrid flows combining detection with updating
Continual learning, test-time adaptation, meta-learning, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning of foundation models for rapid adaptation
Evaluation protocols: prequential evaluation, detection delay (MTTD), false-alarm control (ARL0), missed detection rate, and finance-specific utility metrics
Benchmark recipe specifying drift signatures via four-axis taxonomy, data instantiation, online protocol, and evaluation mapping for reproducible comparison
findings: num: Literature corpus of 289 candidate references narrowed to 174 cited works from 2000-2025
num: Terminological equivalences mapped across machine learning, econometrics, statistics, and quantitative finance for 5 distribution-shift types
num: BOCPD complexity is O(nR_max) with truncation, enabling online use; CUSUM/EWMA are O(n) with O(1) memory for low-latency monitoring
num: PELT achieves O(n) average time for segmentation but is offline; HMM forward filtering is O(nS^2) online
No universally optimal detector or adaptation strategy exists; method selection must align with expected drift type, scale, and dynamics
Evaluation and benchmarking practices remain underdeveloped with limited standardization, weak replicability, and insufficient consideration of operational constraints
Key stability-plasticity trade-off: aggressive adaptation amplifies noise and transaction costs; conservative updates risk sustained degradation after regime changes
Financial time series exhibit strong temporal dependence (autocorrelation, heteroskedasticity) that i.i.d. assumptions within regimes fail to capture

definitions.definition: Change in the conditional distribution P_t(Y|X), i.e., the relationship between inputs and targets
Change in P_t(X) while P_t(Y|X) remains approximately invariant
Change in P_t(Y) (class proportions) while conditional relations are stable
Persistent mode of operation with stable patterns; transitions require persistence, distinctiveness, and possible recurrence
Regime drift: transitions between discrete latent states (e.g., bull/bear). Mechanism drift: fundamental change in causal/structural relationships (e.g., stock-bond correlation sign reversal)
Sequential predictive test where model is trained up to time t, generates predictions, and training set is updated as new observations arrive

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This survey provides the first unified framework organizing drift detection, adaptive learning, and evaluation specifically for financial time series across three typically siloed communities: econometrics, machine learning, and quantitative finance. The four-axis taxonomy (temporal, statistical, spatial, ontological) offers a consistent vocabulary for describing non-stationarity phenomena, directly addressing the terminology fragmentation problem. The five-pillar pipeline connecting representation, detection, adaptation, evaluation, and benchmarking provides a structured design space for practitioners building adaptive financial systems. The evaluation recipe and scenario-coverage benchmark suite constitute a concrete methodological contribution toward reproducible and comparable research in this domain.
directly_justifies: Adopting change-point detection (CUSUM, BOCPD) for monitoring financial time series in Odin's anomaly detection pipeline
Using prequential evaluation and temporal validation protocols for online model assessment
Implementing adaptive retraining strategies when distribution shifts are detected in budget forecasting
Considering multimodal context (macroeconomic indicators, news) alongside price series for better regime awareness
limits: Survey scope excludes MLOps/operational monitoring, temporal fairness, privacy/federated learning, and real-time data revisions
No empirical benchmarks or experimental comparisons are conducted; remains at the conceptual and methodological survey level
Financial examples are illustrative from US/Western markets; emerging market coverage is limited
Deep reinforcement learning and knowledge representation are identified as adjacent but not explored in depth
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: The paper focuses on drift detection and adaptive learning in financial time series, directly intersecting Odin's anomaly detection requirements (codes 8.A and 8.B) and forecasting needs (codes 6.A and 6.B). A systematic scan of the abstract, keywords, section headings, and research questions (RQ1-RQ7) confirmed that the paper's primary contributions are to the drift detection (foundational for anomaly detection) and adaptive learning (core to online forecasting) domains. The evaluation protocol work is also relevant to benchmarking methodology. Classification (5.A) and representation learning (1.A) appeared as supporting themes rather than primary contributions, hence contextual or medium relevance.

limitations: No new empirical experiments or benchmarks are conducted; remains a conceptual survey
Deliberately deprioritizes MLOps, temporal fairness, federated learning, and real-time data revisions
Relies on 289 candidate references narrowed to 174; some relevant works may have been excluded
Financial examples primarily drawn from US/Western developed markets, limiting geographic generalizability
Practical computational constraints and deployment costs are discussed qualitatively but not empirically measured
remember_this: Four-axis taxonomy: temporal, statistical, spatial, ontological
No single best detector; match method to drift type
Prequential evaluation is the gold standard for online settings
Stability-plasticity trade-off central to adaptive learning
Evaluation must cover detection delay, false-alarm control, and economic utility
